I was recently looking into translating a LRAT proof directly into a Lean proof (without reflection). My code is here:
https://git.olsak.net/mirek/lrat-to-lean/src/branch/main

I know that bv_decide works by reflection but I thought that for simple proofs, direct translation (without a detour through Bool & native_decide) could be cleaner. For example

def satProblem3 : SatProblem where
  varNames := #[`a, `b, `c, `d, `p]
  clauses := #[
    [(0, true), (1, true)],    -- 0:  a ∨  b
    [(0, false), (2, false)],  -- 1: ¬a ∨ ¬c
    [(1, false), (3, true)],   -- 2: ¬b ∨  d
    [(1, false), (3, false)],  -- 3: ¬b ∨ ¬d
    [(1, true), (4, true)],    -- 4:  b ∨  p
    [(2, true), (4, false)],   -- 5:  c ∨ ¬p
  ]

def satProof3 : List ActionStd := [
  (.addRat 6 [(0,true), (4,false)] (4,false) #[] #[(4, #[0])]),
  (.addRup 7 [(4,false)] #[6, 5, 1]),
  (.addEmpty 8 #[4, 2, 3]),
]

run_meta debuggingCheck satProblem3 satProof3

translates to

statement: ∀ (a b c d p : Prop),
  ((a → False) → (b → False) → False) →
    (a → c → False) →
      (b → (d → False) → False) →
        (b → d → False) → ((b → False) → (p → False) → False) → ((c → False) → p → False) → False

proof: fun a b c d p hyp_0 hyp_1 hyp_2 hyp_3 hyp_4 hyp_5 =>
  let tree1 := a → False;
  have himpl := fun htree1 =>
    have hn_a := htree1;
    fun hn_b => hyp_0 hn_a hn_b;
  let p_1 := p ∧ (tree1 → False);
  have p_update0 := And.left;
  have hyp_4 := fun hn_b hn_p =>
    hn_p ⟨Classical.byContradiction fun hn_p => hyp_4 hn_b hn_p, fun htree1 => himpl htree1 hn_b⟩;
  have clause_6 := fun h_p hn_a => h_p.2 hn_a;
  have hyp_5 := fun hn_c h_p => hyp_5 hn_c (p_update0 h_p);
  have clause_7 := fun h_p =>
    have h_a := Classical.byContradiction (clause_6 h_p);
    have h_c := Classical.byContradiction fun hn_c => hyp_5 hn_c h_p;
    hyp_1 h_a h_c;
  have h_b := Classical.byContradiction fun hn_b => hyp_4 hn_b clause_7;
  have h_d := Classical.byContradiction (hyp_2 h_b);
  hyp_3 h_b h_d

I wanted to ask for help with using bv_decide machinery for connecting with a SAT solver. My main action structure should be really similar to the one in bv_decide, perhaps except I am indexing from zero.

I would be interested in

  • calling a SAT solver on a raw SAT problem stored in Lean, and receiving the steps in Lean's Actions
  • benchmarking / testing my translation on some problems that bv_decide was tested with to have an idea about the slowdown / proof size using the Lean proof approach.

The SAT solver interaction is handled with this function https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/a36459511109c7867ddf80d3170c2f005773d02f/src/Lean/Elab/Tactic/BVDecide/Frontend/LRAT.lean#L133-L152. If you want problems that bv_decide was tested on you can take any of the tests that are prefixed with bv_. Getting direct access to the SAT formula they produce is not really trivial but you can capture the temp file they are put into or just patch core to print them for you I'd guess. bv_decide was also extensively evaluated on the 46000 problems in QF_BV SMT-LIB and solves around 44900 of them under competition rules at the moment (the best SMT solver in the category is ~500 problems ahead of bv_decide).

The thing with this kind of approach is that there are basically three approaches you can take:

  1. Just decide +revert the formula
  2. What you are doing
  3. What bv_decide is doing

I've been wondering for a while whether there is a set of problems that decide +revert times out on while the LRAT->Lean translation still manages to produce reasonable results, that would be the one niche where this kind of approach would fit. The issue here is that for non trivially sized SAT problems the LRAT proofs also explode. bv_decide routinely deals with LRAT proofs that are in the 100s of MB to the GB range.

Note that one big motivation for proof by reflection in bv_decide was not only the LRAT checking but also the bitblasting infrastructure, developing a bitblaster that does not work by reflection but instead produces explicit proof terms would be a large undertaking on its own. In particular given that bv_decide fully shares the circuit it creates during the procedure.

Maybe on an interesting side note: I've also started work on a bv_decide variation that does not rely on native_decide though rather as a low priority experiment for now.

I am just a bit confused by one thing: runExternal returns a String of numbers (even if the original proof is in binary format). I found that another function LratCert.load can load a List of IntAction from a file again but I don't see a direct conversion into Array IntAction. I could load it from the file again but I don't understand why when it was already loaded by runExternal. What is a straightforward way to get an array of IntActions from the SAT solver call?

The reason for that is that the kernel only has native support for storing String literals efficiently. So if I would put the fully expanded LRAT proof as an Array IntAction into the olean file when the proof itself is say 1GB large in binary format we would get a several gigabyte large Lean term for the kernel to check in O(n) or even worse time. Type checking a string literal on the other hand is always O(1) regardless of its size. For that reason bv_decide:

  1. Loads the proof from the SAT solver
  2. trims it and inserts deletions
  3. then turns it into a string again
  4. puts that string into a declaration for the kernel to typecheck
  5. reparses the string during the proof by reflection in native code
  6. runs the checker

without this indirection checking proofs that are non trivially sized is basically impossible so the API isn't built to support it. You can either go with it an reparse the string you get from runExternal yourself or write your own variant of run external that acts differently.

Sure, and what is a straightforward way of parsing the string? I can see LRAT.parseLRATProof but that goes from ByteArray instead of a string...

And I also wanted to ask about where I can find the tests. I found some tests here: https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/tree/master/tests/lean/ but I don't see any that start with bv_

String and ByteArray can easily be converted into each other, there is still an O(n) conversion cost between the two but that will be eliminated in the near to mid term future.

Do you know if some of the tests is testing the different kinds of LRAT steps? I would like to check if I am translating it from IntAction correctly but the RAT step is usually not used by cadical...

It doesn't test the RAT steps no. Partially because CaDiCaL doesn't produce them but also because the whole thing with RAT seems to be messed up. The original paper about LRAT has either a mistake or a very weird design decision for the grammar of RAT steps and there doesn't even exist a specification for how they are encoded in binary.
(the parser I wrote is a guess based on extrapolating the RUP format but I truly have no idea whether it would work...after all nobody produces them)
Oh, I see. So the main point of using LRAT is the specific encoding into numbers, not that it has RAT.
The main point of using LRAT is the L part for checking time. With things like DRAT you actually have algorithmically non trivial checking logic (if you want to be efficient)

Henrik Böving said:

Note that one big motivation for proof by reflection in bv_decide was not only the LRAT checking but also the bitblasting infrastructure, developing a bitblaster that does not work by reflection but instead produces explicit proof terms would be a large undertaking on its own. In particular given that bv_decide fully shares the circuit it creates during the procedure.

To be honest, it still feels to me that going through Bools & BitVectors is a bit of a detour for my purposes, and I don't control it as well as I would like. I have some ideas of doing SAT preparation on the Prop level which could be easier. I will let you know when I have something again.
the conversion to booleans is just to have a unique normal form to rewrite into and during the design of the reflection procedure it turned out that going to Bool as opposed to Prop was easier.

Note that rewriting plays a pretty huge role in bv_decide as well. It's able to solve many benchmarks from SMT-LIB without ever taking it as far as even launching the SAT solver by applying domain specific rewrites copied from Bitwuzla.
Is the SAT problem also stored in the file? I can see the LRAT file but not the original problem... Also, is there a parser from DIMACS?
(I am asking for the tests / benchmarks)
What is "the file" here?
I meant "a file". File with the SAT problem as got translated from a Lean goal upon bv_decide call.
Sure there is a temp file created while invoking the SAT solver as I mentioned above.

This code only deals with the Lrat tempfile right?

@[builtin_tactic Lean.Parser.Tactic.bvDecide]
def evalBvDecide : Tactic := fun
  | `(tactic| bv_decide $cfg:optConfig) => do
    let cfg ← elabBVDecideConfig cfg
    IO.FS.withTempFile fun _ lratFile => do
      let cfg ← BVDecide.Frontend.TacticContext.new lratFile cfg
      liftMetaFinishingTactic fun g => do
        discard <| bvDecide g cfg
  | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax

if you intend to import the problem sure, but that should be trivial. In particular the parser doesn't have to be Lean of course, surely someone has written this in python and you can just use it to generate the Lean file with the input you need.

Okay, so I tried the "stress" test

theorem t5 {x y : BitVec 4096} (h : x = y) : (~~~x) &&& y = (~~~y) &&& x := by
  bv_decide

which gets solved by a sat-solver & verified by bv_decide in a fraction of a second. It takes about 5s to get converted to a Lean expression, and about 6 minutes to get checked by a kernel (if my interpretation is correct about what is happening at the end of a run_meta block containing addDecl, of course I had to increase the recursion depth).

Perhaps kernel doesn't like deep expressions, and would be more efficient if I stored the individual clauses as global constants? Or another kernel in the kernel arena could be more efficient? Anyway, I admit the efficiency gap is currently larger than I expected. What are the stress tests that decide +revert have troubles with?

If you want a real stress test try bv_decide_mod, that one even takes bv_decide a while to crunch (though mostly because it waits for the SAT solver)

decide +revert is essentially bruteforce so at some amount of boolean variables it will automatically start giving in
